prompt: A purchase fails somewhere between the button and the confirmation. Which question does the whole-system view tell you to ask first?

options.text: Which boundary did not preserve the intended request, identity, data, or response
Which process raised the error, since that is where the failure happened
options.feedback: A process is where a failure surfaced, which is not the same as where the intended thing stopped being preserved. A web app is the coordinated behaviour of the arrangement, not any single process.

options.text: Whether the fault is on the browser side or the server side
options.feedback: A typical interaction crosses presentation code, network infrastructure, server-side application logic and one or more data systems. Two sides are not enough categories to hold the answer.

options.text: Which component is at fault, so that component can be fixed
options.feedback: Naming a component only searches the boxes. Every arrow between them is a contract and a possible failure boundary too, and a question about boxes never reaches those.

explanation: What the map buys is a first question with an owner attached: which boundary did not preserve the intended request, identity, data, or response. Naming a process, a side or a component answers something narrower than what was asked.

prompt: Match each responsibility to the part of the arrangement that holds it.

pairs.left: Presents documents and controls, and sends protocol messages
Terminates secure connections and routes traffic
Validates requests and coordinates business behaviour
Preserves facts
Keeps the whole arrangement operable

explanation: Each part answers for one kind of thing, which is what makes “which boundary did not preserve what” a question anybody can act on. The two distractors are genuine participants — a backend publishes follow-up work to a queue and is a client to a payment API — but neither of them owns any of the five responsibilities listed here.

prompt: Order the steps of one purchase, from the browser's first move to the updated screen.

steps.text: Browser sends an HTTP request with session credentials
Backend authenticates the caller, then authorizes the action
Backend validates input, then executes a transaction
Backend publishes follow-up work and returns a representation
Frontend reconciles the response with local state and updates the page

explanation: Two things in that order are easy to lose. Identity is established before the action is authorized and before the input is validated, so both of those run on a caller who has already been identified. And the exchange is not finished when the representation is returned: published follow-up work lands in a system the response need not mention, and the frontend still has to reconcile what came back.

prompt: A dependency is overloaded and calls to it are timing out. Someone proposes retrying every failed call automatically. What does that proposal risk?

options.text: Amplifying the overload, and duplicating effects
Nothing — the calls failed, so there is nothing to duplicate
options.feedback: A call that failed for the caller is not a call that did nothing. Duplicate submissions and partial writes are both on the list of common failures.

options.text: Expired certificates, because each retry renegotiates the connection
options.feedback: Expired certificates are a common failure, but nothing here connects them to retrying. Taking any entry off the list is not the same as reasoning about this one.

options.text: Changing one side of a contract before the other
options.feedback: That is a deployment failure mode. A retry repeats a message; it does not change a contract.

explanation: A retry can repair transient failure, or amplify overload and duplicate effects — one mechanism with both outcomes available. With the dependency already overloaded, amplification is the outcome the proposal invites.

prompt: A team moves confirmation work out of the request and into a background job — one more boundary. What does that boundary charge for the independent change it enables?

options.text: Latency
Failure modes
Security policy
Operational work
Independent change or scale
Fewer parts to operate

explanation: An added boundary enables independent change or scale, and it adds latency, failure modes, security policy, and operational work. The two wrong options are the other side of that trade: independent change or scale is what the boundary buys rather than what it costs, and it is bought with operational work rather than by reducing it.

back: A distributed system with a human-facing browser interface. A typical interaction crosses presentation code, network infrastructure, server-side application logic, and one or more data systems, and the visible page is only the edge of it.

Each arrow between the parts is a contract and a possible failure boundary — the half of the map the boxes hide. A component may play several roles across those arrows: a backend is a server to the browser and a client to a database or a payment API.
HTTP defines the uniform semantics shared across its versions, which is why one trace can describe the exchange without naming a version.

Server-rendered or client-rendered UI, a synchronous request or a background job, a relational database or another model, one deployable unit or several services, a managed platform or self-operated infrastructure — the important choices are choices about where the boundaries go.

front: A success response is not the outcome
back: For `POST /orders`, correctness may require a durable order, exactly one charge effect, inventory policy, a traceable audit record, and a UI state that distinguishes “pending” from “failed”. The web app is the coordinated behaviour, not any single process.

prompt: A host answers packets and accepts a connection, but the page still will not load. What have those two checks established?

options.text: That the network path is clean end to end
options.feedback: Two successful samples are not a clean path — packet loss and connection exhaustion are still on the list of things that go wrong. And even a flawless path would say nothing about HTTP.

options.text: Routing and basic reachability, but nothing about HTTP behaviour
That DNS is configured correctly, since the host responded
options.feedback: You reached it by address, so name resolution was never exercised. DNS is still a suspect.

options.text: That the application is up and the browser is at fault
options.feedback: A web app can be unavailable even when its host is perfectly reachable. Nothing here has looked at the app yet.

explanation: Each check proves a property of one layer and the layers below it. A network can deliver packets while an HTTP request fails, so reachability says nothing about whether HTTP behaviour is correct.

prompt: HTTP is defined as a stateless application-level request-response protocol. What does that make the login session your app keeps?

options.text: An added mechanism, built on top of a protocol that carries nothing between requests
A feature of HTTP that switches on once the user authenticates
options.feedback: Statelessness is not a mode HTTP leaves. Whatever continuity your app has between requests, your app added it.

options.text: A property of the transport connection underneath
options.feedback: A transport connection associates endpoint addresses and ports. Application state is not its job, and connections may be short-lived by design.

options.text: A sign that the app has been built incorrectly
options.feedback: Sessions are normal and necessary. The point is only that they sit above HTTP rather than inside it.

explanation: HTTP is explicitly stateless, so application sessions are something built on top of it. That is also why “how much application state is coupled to a particular process” is a live design decision rather than a settled one.

prompt: Match each decision a developer makes to the layer of the stack it is made at.

pairs.left: Where to terminate TLS
Which intermediaries may cache content
Long-lived or short-lived connections
How much state is coupled to one process

explanation: Naming the layer a decision belongs to is most of what the stack is for. None of these four decisions lands on routing or the physical network, which is why those two appear here only as distractors.

back: The internet is a network of interconnected networks, moving packets between interfaces. The web is an application system built on that connectivity, using URLs to identify resources, HTTP to exchange representations, and browsers as general-purpose clients.
HTTP is explicitly a stateless application-level request-response protocol, so nothing in it carries information from one request to the next. Application sessions are an added mechanism on top.
The distributed hierarchy that resolves names to addresses. It is the step a request that works by IP but not by name never got to exercise.

front: A reasoning stack, not an implementation
back: The layer diagram is a reasoning tool, not a claim that every implementation has identical layers. What it fixes is the direction of dependence: each layer relies on services below it and exposes a narrower abstraction above. The same dependence runs through a page load, which is why one step can fail on its own terms while the rest look healthy.
More intermediaries can improve reach, security and caching, and the same intermediaries complicate diagnosis and trust — proxy policy being one of the ways a request fails.

prompt: Order the six messages of one request-response exchange.

steps.text: Frontend to edge: request, credentials and trace context
Backend to data store: query or transaction
Backend to edge: status, headers and content

explanation: The request travels down the participants and the response comes back up the same three hops. Every one of the six is a place the exchange can stop — the three on the way back no less than the three on the way out.

prompt: Match each responsibility to the participant that holds it.

pairs.left: Attach headers and apply credential rules
Terminate TLS or serve a cached representation
Establish request context, then authorize
Answer a query or run a transaction

explanation: Naming the participant that owns a responsibility is what makes a boundary check possible: an edge that serves a cached representation means the backend never saw the message at all. DNS resolution and connection pooling are in the path too, but they are work that may not happen — reused from caches or pools — rather than participants that decide anything about the message.

prompt: A checkout has a two-second user deadline. Which of these follow from budgeting the path end to end rather than hop by hop?

options.text: Reserve a portion of the two seconds for connection, edge, application, database and response transfer
Refuse to start a five-second payment call once 1.8 seconds have already gone
Give every hop its own two-second timeout so no single hop is the bottleneck
Retry any request that overruns its portion, so the user still gets an answer

explanation: Deadlines are chosen end to end, not independently at every hop. Per-hop timeouts that are each generous on their own terms are how a path ends up with no budget at all, which rules out the third option. The fourth ignores two constraints at once: a blanket retry is how retry storms start, and retrying an operation that is neither idempotent nor queryable can commit the work twice.

prompt: Requests are slow, but the application's own timing shows it handling them quickly. Which part of the path does that point at?
hints: The application only starts its clock once it has the request.
The time went somewhere before the code you instrumented.
explanation: Queueing before application code is a standard failure mode, and it hides from application timing by definition — the clock the application keeps starts after the wait is already over. The symptom eliminates application logic and points at whatever held the request before it.

back: A request carries a method and a target; a response carries a status and optional content. Credentials, trace context, caching and deadlines are arrangement built around those two messages rather than parts of them.

A retry that reuses the same idempotency key lets the server return the original outcome instead of doing the work a second time. It is what turns a timeout from an unknown outcome into a question you can ask again.
Streaming reduces time to first content and complicates error replacement: once content has started arriving, an error can no longer simply replace it.
Caching saves work and adds invalidation and privacy rules. Both obligations arrive with the saving, not later.
A `200` response can still contain the wrong business result. The status describes the exchange, not the correctness of the outcome carried inside it.

prompt: An HTTP origin is distinguished by scheme, host and port. Which of these changes leaves the origin the same?

options.text: Changing the path from `/orders` to `/orders/open`
Changing the scheme from `http` to `https`
options.feedback: The scheme is part of the origin, so those are two different origins even though the host and the path never moved.

options.text: Moving the app from `app.example.com` to `www.example.com`
options.feedback: The host is part of the origin. This is the migration that touches DNS records, certificates, cookie scope and everything else defined on an origin.

options.text: Serving the same host on a different port
options.feedback: The port is part of the origin too. All three of scheme, host and port have to match.

explanation: Scheme, host and port make an origin; the path and the query do not. That is why moving a resource within a host is cheap and moving it to another host is not.

prompt: Query parameters are appropriate for selecting a representation and unsafe for secrets. What property of URLs makes them unsafe?
accept: they appear in logs and history
URLs appear in logs and history
they end up in logs and history
hints: Think about where a URL is written down after the request is over.
Two places keep it: one on the server side, one in the browser.
explanation: URLs appear in logs and history, so anything in the query outlives the request in places nobody audited. The path and query being addressed to the application does not make them private.

prompt: A DNS record was changed an hour ago, and some clients still reach the old address. What does that show?

options.text: Resolution can follow caches and delegated name servers, so nothing guarantees a change is instantly global
The change was applied incorrectly, since DNS is authoritative
options.feedback: An authoritative record is not the same thing as the answer a client currently holds. Caches and delegated name servers sit between the two.

options.text: The old server is refusing to give up the name
options.feedback: Servers do not hold names. What is holding the old answer is the resolution path, not the machine at the end of it.

options.text: A shorter time-to-live would have made the change instant
options.feedback: Short TTLs speed routing changes and increase lookup traffic — and still never guarantee instant global change.

explanation: DNS resolution can follow caches and delegated name servers, so an answer describes what some resolver holds rather than what is authoritative right now. Short TTLs shift the tradeoff — faster routing changes, more lookup traffic — without ever guaranteeing instant global change.

prompt: Match each symptom to the mechanism it implicates.

pairs.left: The name still resolves to the old address
The certificate is not valid for this host
A forwarded host field is trusted unchecked
One page loads content over both schemes

explanation: Each symptom narrows to one of the four cooperating mechanisms rather than to all of them. Mixed HTTP and HTTPS content is the one people misfile: it implicates the scheme in the URLs a page emits, not the server that served the page. Cookie scope and OAuth redirect URIs are things an origin migration breaks, but no symptom listed here points at either.

back: Negotiates cryptographic parameters, and is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery.
Many requests may share one connection without sharing application meaning. A connection is a pipe, not a session.
They improve linking and caching, which is why a path worth publishing is a path worth keeping.
Moving a host touches DNS records, certificates, cookie scope, CORS policy, OAuth redirect URIs, canonical links, caches and monitoring — an origin migration, not a text replacement.

Convenient, and it moves the boundary: the internal hops past the edge still need an explicit trust model of their own. And the certificate itself proves control of a name under the certificate system, not that the application behind it is benign.

prompt: `GET /reports/monthly` returned a cached PDF last week and a redirect to object storage today. What changed?

options.text: The representation and its delivery, while the resource stayed the same
The resource, since a redirect is a different kind of thing from a document
options.feedback: The resource is the conceptual target the URI identifies. It is still the monthly report — a redirect is one more way of delivering a representation of it.

options.text: Nothing a client can observe, so the difference does not matter
options.feedback: A client certainly observes it. The point is not that the change is invisible; it is that the change was the server's to make.

options.text: The identifier's meaning, which now names object storage
options.feedback: The URL still names the monthly report. Had it named the storage, this migration would have changed the identifier too — which is the failure the design exists to avoid.

explanation: A resource is the conceptual target identified by a URI; a representation is transferable information about that resource. The current representation and its delivery mechanism are separate design decisions, so changing them is not changing the resource.

prompt: Match each design choice to what it buys and what it costs.

pairs.left: Coarse representations
Fine-grained resources
Server authority
Optimistic client state

distractors: Stable nouns and generic HTTP behavior
explanation: Each choice buys something at a stated price, and none of them has a default answer. Server authority is the one whose price you have to read off its alternative: what it gives up is the responsiveness optimistic client state can buy. The two distractors are real benefits — of resource-oriented and action-oriented designs respectively — but they belong to the choice of style, not to any of the four tradeoffs listed here.

prompt: Which of these break a client even though the server's own code is correct?

options.text: A URL that encoded an implementation detail which later changed
A status code that does not match the outcome
A representation that silently omits information needed to interpret it
An account assembled from several stores rather than read from one row
A response format changing from HTML to JSON under content negotiation

explanation: The first three are failures of the boundary rather than of the logic behind it: the client was told something untrue, or told too little, or made to depend on a detail it should never have seen. The last two are the arrangement working — HTTP deliberately hides resource implementation, and negotiating a format is what content negotiation is for. A client that breaks on either had inferred undocumented behaviour.

back: The method communicates the requested action; the target names what the action concerns.

Clients select methods, targets, fields and acceptable formats. Servers interpret those semantics, enforce policy, and choose a status and a representation. Both are roles in one interaction rather than kinds of machine: the same process is a server to a browser and a client to a payment provider.
Content negotiation, conditional requests, redirects and caching let a single resource model support different clients and efficient reuse.
It can represent an account assembled from several stores, calculated at request time, and formatted as HTML or JSON, all without the identifier changing.

Resource implementation, behind messages and representations — the uniform boundary that lets independently implemented components interoperate. It can hide multiplicity too: what you call the server may be a chain of proxies and services with different policy.
